title: Southern Celestial Wayfinder
caption: The SOAR Telescope under the Milky Way, Cerro Pachón
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way seems to pour out of an open dome and spill across a colourful sky. The dome houses the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) Telescope on Cerro Pachón in Chile, operated by NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). Near the horizon, a wash of yellow and green comes from airglow mixed with light pollution from nearby villages. Where those two colours meet, at lower left, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds shine through.

Near the centre of the frame sits the constellation Crux, also called the Southern Cross. It can be found by its red star at the top of the cross and the three nearby blue stars that complete the shape.

European and Pacific Islander navigators have steered by this group of stars for centuries. It plays a part like Polaris in the north, but where Polaris guides travellers north, Crux points roughly towards the South Pole.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by Tomas Slovinský. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds would look fainter to someone at the site.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The photograph is huge, at 900 megapixels, and was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition to all of NOIRLab's sites. Its photographer, Tomas Slovinský, is a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.
alt: The Milky Way rising from the open dome of the SOAR Telescope into a sky tinted yellow and green near the horizon, with the Magellanic Clouds at lower left.
